claim: AMP training for aerial humanoid robot (iRonCub) walk-fly transitions required ~2 hours with 4096 parallel agents on NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000 using Isaac Gym.
stance_target: AMP training wall-clock time for legged locomotion on high-end professional GPU
scope_conditions: iRonCub aerial humanoid, 23 joints, Isaac Gym, flat/terrain scenarios
quoted_support: 'We trained 4096 agents using PPO, controlled at 60 hz. The training requires ~2 hours on an NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000.'

claim: PPO mini-batch size of 32768 is used with 4096 parallel agents in AMP walk-fly training.
stance_target: PPO batch sizes used in massively parallel AMP training
quoted_support: Table I (PPO parameters): 'Mini-batch size: 32768, Number of actors: 4096'

claim: The walk-fly AMP system uses small motion datasets: walking from CMU human mocap retargeted via IK, flying from trajectory optimization — no explicit clip counts or dataset size in steps stated.
stance_target: AMP demo dataset source and size for locomotion training
quoted_support: 'Walking motions are produced from recorded mocap clip and retargeted to the iRonCub model using inverse kinematics... Trajectory optimization for aerial humanoid robots produces flying motions containing the full state.'

claim: The AMP walk-fly system trains stable policies (low variance across 10 runs) with ~2 hours on a Quadro RTX 6000, suggesting AMP convergence is fast and robust for this task class.
stance_target: AMP training stability and convergence speed
scope_conditions: iRonCub AMP, Isaac Gym, 10 training runs
quoted_support: 'The curves show a small variance, demonstrating the stability of the training.'

claim: No BC pretrain stage, no DR finetune stage breakdown — the walk-fly AMP paper reports a single 2-hour training run as the complete budget.
stance_target: AMP training pipeline stages for legged locomotion
quoted_support: Section IV-B: 'The training requires ~2 hours on an NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000. The training parameters are shown in Tab. I.' No pretrain or finetune stages described.
